source_landscape: Well documented (Wikipedia 'WannaCry ransomware attack', Microsoft MSRC MS17-010/CVE-2017-0144/0145, NSA-leak retrospectives, technical analyses of EternalBlue internals, and the 2026-09-05 canonical run whose supported claims this sheet enumerates). Outbreak May 2017; EternalBlue exploit of SMBv1 patched by MS17-010 (March 2017); roughly 200,000 machines across ~150 countries; kill-switch domain registration halted the spread.
note: DRAFT 2026-09-05 — facts checked against web sources by agent. expected_claims enumerate the supported claims of the 2026-09-05 canonical run atomically (a correct report asserting its own legitimate details must get credit, not a precision penalty). Each entry was audited against the public record, not taken on the pipeline's word; facts are phrased positively (no negation) so polarity checks do not reject equivalent claims. OWNER MUST AUDIT before pilot numbers are meaningful.

expected_claims.statement: EternalBlue is an exploit that targets MS17-010, which patches flaws in the Windows SMBv1 protocol.
expected_claims.note: Core mechanism; independently corroborated.

expected_claims.statement: EternalBlue was developed by the United States National Security Agency and was released publicly in April 2017 by a group known as the Shadow Brokers.
expected_claims.note: NSA origin + Shadow Brokers leak; well documented.

expected_claims.statement: The Shadow Brokers released EternalBlue in April 2017.
expected_claims.variant_of: EternalBlue was developed by the United States National Security Agency and was released publicly in April 2017 by a group known as the Shadow Brokers.
expected_claims.note: Alternate phrasing of the leak fact.

expected_claims.statement: Microsoft released the MS17-010 security update in March 2017, about two months before the WannaCry outbreak.
expected_claims.note: Patch timing explains the patching driver.

expected_claims.statement: The WannaCry ransomware worm spread in May 2017 by exploiting EternalBlue on unpatched Windows systems.
expected_claims.note: Attack path; the canonical question's core.

expected_claims.statement: WannaCry infected roughly 200,000 computers across more than 150 countries in May 2017.
expected_claims.note: Scale; widely reported estimates.

expected_claims.statement: WannaCry spread very fast because it was a self-propagating worm and because many organizations had not installed the available MS17-010 patch.
expected_claims.note: The 'why so fast' answer: worm behavior + slow patching.

expected_claims.statement: WannaCry performed automatic network scanning to find vulnerable machines.
expected_claims.note: Worm propagation mechanism; encyclopedic.

expected_claims.statement: WannaCry spread without requiring any user interaction.
expected_claims.note: No-click worm property; encyclopedic.

expected_claims.statement: The spread of WannaCry was halted after a researcher registered the worm's hardcoded kill-switch domain.
expected_claims.note: Kill-switch account; naming Marcus Hutchins optional.

expected_claims.statement: WannaCry encrypted user files and demanded Bitcoin payments on unpatched Windows systems.
expected_claims.note: Ransomware behavior; encyclopedic.

expected_claims.statement: Systems that had installed the MS17-010 patch, released in March 2017, were protected from EternalBlue-based propagation.
expected_claims.note: Causal claim about patching; phrased positively (immune/protected paraphrases match).

expected_claims.statement: EternalBlue allows an unauthenticated attacker to send crafted packets to a vulnerable machine over port 445.
expected_claims.note: Exploit mechanics; documented in technical writeups.

expected_claims.statement: EternalBlue exploits size parameter mismatches that cause out-of-bounds writes in the Windows kernel memory pool.
expected_claims.note: Internals detail from technical analyses.

expected_claims.statement: EternalBlue uses a technique called Pool Grooming to manipulate kernel memory.
expected_claims.note: Internals detail from technical analyses.

expected_claims.statement: DoublePulsar is a kernel-level backdoor that can be delivered via EternalBlue.
expected_claims.note: Well-documented pairing in technical analyses.

expected_claims.statement: WannaCry arrived about 28 days after the Shadow Brokers released EternalBlue.
expected_claims.note: Derived from the leak (14 April) and outbreak (12 May) dates.

expected_claims.statement: WannaCry achieved global distribution within hours of its May 2017 outbreak.
expected_claims.note: Speed claim consistent with the canonical run.

expected_claims.statement: WannaCry's spread was modeled using an epidemic spread metric known as R0.
expected_claims.note: Modeling claim from technical writeups rather than a directly observable fact; low gold expectation.

expected_claims.statement: Widespread delays in applying the MS17-010 patch left hundreds of thousands of systems vulnerable to EternalBlue.
expected_claims.note: Patching-driver scale claim.
